::: proof
Write $\mu_i \eqdef t_i \expf{\b_0 + \b_1 x_i}$ for observation $i$'s mean.
Each $y_i$ has a Poisson distribution with mean $\mu_i$,
so the [log-likelihood](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/intro-MLEs.html#def-loglik) is

$$
\ba
\llik(\b_0, \b_1)
&= \sumin \logf{\frac{\mu_i^{y_i} \expf{-\mu_i}}{y_i!}}
&& \text{(independence; Poisson PMF)} \\
&= \sumin \paren{y_i \logf{\mu_i} - \mu_i - \logf{y_i!}}
&& \text{(log of a product and quotient)} \\
&= \sumin \paren{y_i \paren{\logf{t_i} + \b_0 + \b_1 x_i} - \mu_i - \logf{y_i!}}
&& \text{(} \logf{\mu_i} = \logf{t_i} + \b_0 + \b_1 x_i \text{)}
\ea
$$

Each mean has derivatives
$\deriv{\b_0} \mu_i = \mu_i$
and
$\deriv{\b_1} \mu_i = \mu_i x_i$
(chain rule for $\expf{\cdot}$),
so the [score equations](https://morrison-lab.github.io/sds/intro-MLEs.html#def-score-equation) are:

$$
\ba
0 = \deriv{\b_0} \llik
&= \sumin \paren{y_i - \mu_i}
&& \text{(differentiate term by term)} \\
0 = \deriv{\b_1} \llik
&= \sumin x_i \paren{y_i - \mu_i}
&& \text{(differentiate term by term)}
\ea
$$

In the second score equation, the terms with $x_i = 0$ vanish,
and every remaining term has mean $\mu_i = t_i \expf{\b_0 + \b_1}$:

$$
\ba
0
&= \sum_{i: x_i = 1} \paren{y_i - t_i \expf{\b_0 + \b_1}}
&& \text{(drop the } x_i = 0 \text{ terms)} \\
&= D_1 - T_1 \expf{\b_0 + \b_1}
&& \text{(definitions of } D_1 \text{ and } T_1 \text{)} \\
\expf{\b_0 + \b_1}
&= \frac{D_1}{T_1}
&& \text{(solve for } \expf{\b_0 + \b_1} \text{)}
\ea
$$

Subtracting the second score equation from the first
leaves the terms with $x_i = 0$,
whose means are $\mu_i = t_i \expf{\b_0}$:

$$
\ba
0
&= \sum_{i: x_i = 0} \paren{y_i - t_i \expf{\b_0}}
&& \text{(first equation minus second)} \\
&= D_0 - T_0 \expf{\b_0}
&& \text{(definitions of } D_0 \text{ and } T_0 \text{)} \\
\expf{\b_0}
&= \frac{D_0}{T_0}
&& \text{(solve for } \expf{\b_0} \text{)}
\ea
$$

Both solutions are positive because $D_k > 0$,
so the logarithm gives a unique stationary point $(\eb_0, \eb_1)$.
That stationary point is the maximum,
because $\llik$ is strictly concave.
To see this concavity,
write $x_{i0} \eqdef 1$ and $x_{i1} \eqdef x_i$,
so that both score equations read
$\deriv{\b_j} \llik = \sumin x_{ij} \paren{y_i - \mu_i}$.
Differentiating again:

$$
\ba
\frac{\partial^2 \llik}{\partial \b_j \, \partial \b_k}
&= \deriv{\b_k} \sumin x_{ij} \paren{y_i - \mu_i}
&& \text{(differentiate the score)} \\
&= -\sumin x_{ij} \deriv{\b_k} \mu_i
&& \text{(} y_i \text{ and } x_{ij} \text{ do not depend on } \b_k \text{)} \\
&= -\sumin x_{ij} x_{ik} \mu_i
&& \text{(} \deriv{\b_k} \mu_i = \mu_i x_{ik} \text{)}
\ea
$$

Let $\mu_{\cdot k} \eqdef \sum_{i: x_i = k} \mu_i > 0$ be group $k$'s total mean.
Because $x_i^2 = x_i$ for $x_i \in \cb{0, 1}$,
$\sumin x_i^2 \mu_i = \sumin x_i \mu_i = \mu_{\cdot 1}$
and $\sumin \mu_i = \mu_{\cdot 0} + \mu_{\cdot 1}$,
so the [Hessian](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/vector-calculus.html#def-hessian) of $\llik$ is

$$
\underbrace{\hessian}_{2 \times 2}
= -\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
\sumin \mu_i & \sumin x_i \mu_i \\
\sumin x_i \mu_i & \sumin x_i^2 \mu_i
\end{bmatrix}}_{2 \times 2}
= -\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
\mu_{\cdot 0} + \mu_{\cdot 1} & \mu_{\cdot 1} \\
\mu_{\cdot 1} & \mu_{\cdot 1}
\end{bmatrix}}_{2 \times 2}
$$ {#eq-pois-two-group-hessian}

Its upper-left entry $-(\mu_{\cdot 0} + \mu_{\cdot 1})$ is negative
and its determinant is

$$
\ba
\det \hessian
&= (-1)^2 \det \begin{bmatrix}
\mu_{\cdot 0} + \mu_{\cdot 1} & \mu_{\cdot 1} \\
\mu_{\cdot 1} & \mu_{\cdot 1}
\end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(} \det(-\mat{A}) = (-1)^2 \det \mat{A} \text{ for a } 2 \times 2 \text{ matrix)} \\
&= (\mu_{\cdot 0} + \mu_{\cdot 1}) \mu_{\cdot 1} - \mu_{\cdot 1}^2
&& \text{(} 2 \times 2 \text{ determinant formula; } (-1)^2 = 1 \text{)} \\
&= \mu_{\cdot 0} \mu_{\cdot 1} + \mu_{\cdot 1}^2 - \mu_{\cdot 1}^2
&& \text{(distribute)} \\
&= \mu_{\cdot 0} \mu_{\cdot 1}
&& \text{(cancel)} \\
&> 0
&& \text{(both group totals are positive)}
\ea
$$

so $\hessian$ is negative definite at every $(\b_0, \b_1)$,
which makes $\llik$ strictly concave.

Finally, the rate ratio estimate follows by division:

$$
\ba
\erateratio(1 : 0)
&= \frac{\el(1)}{\el(0)}
&& \text{(definition of rate ratio)} \\
&= \frac{\expf{\eb_0 + \eb_1}}{\expf{\eb_0}}
&& \text{(fitted rate function)} \\
&= \expf{\eb_1}
&& \text{(quotient rule for exponentials)} \\
&= \frac{D_1 / T_1}{D_0 / T_0}
&& \text{(substitute the two solutions)}
\ea
$$

:::
